summary: For ages 11–12, teach inverse operations (add↔subtract, multiply↔divide by a non-zero number, square↔square-root for non-negative numbers) as a way to UNDO calculations — both to check results and to solve for an unknown by isolating it. Core principles: undoing a multi-step process reverses both the operations AND their order (last done, first undone); and 'do the same to both sides' keeps an equation balanced. This is the concrete foundation for solving and rearranging equations. Build the do/undo intuition through function-machine and balance-scale work, then consolidate and probe reasoning.
misconceptions: Undoing operations in the WRONG order (undoing the × before the + in a two-step machine) — not reversing the order of operations.
Applying the inverse to only one side of an equation, breaking the balance.
Confusing inverse (undo) with commutative/associative relationships, or thinking subtraction 'undoes' multiplication.
Believing squaring and square-rooting are perfect inverses without the ± / non-negative subtlety.
Treating 'inverse' as merely reversing the numbers (12÷156 to check 156÷12) rather than applying the inverse operation.

activities.title: Function machine: run it forwards, then run it backwards
steps: Build a two-step machine, e.g. '×3 then +2'. Drop in an input (say 5) and record the output (17).
Now recover the original input WITHOUT being told it: work out which operation to undo first and which second. (Undo +2 first → 15, then ÷3 → 5.)
Deliberately try undoing in the forward order instead (÷3 first, then −2) and check whether you get back the start number. Notice it does NOT return 5 — this shows why the order must reverse.
State the rule in your own words: to undo a chain, reverse both the operations and their order (last done is first undone).

If a live model is available, flip the machine into REVERSE mode so each step is automatically swapped for its inverse and reordered, and compare it with a manual attempt that undoes the steps in the forward order; that wrong-order attempt visibly fails to return the starting value.
activities.insight: Each operation is undone by its inverse, and to undo a sequence you must reverse BOTH the operations and their order.

activities.title: Balance scale: solving one-step unknowns by keeping both sides equal
steps: Look at a balance representing □ + 7 = 20. Decide which inverse isolates the unknown (subtract 7).
Apply that inverse to BOTH sides and read off □ = 20 − 7 = 13.
Try applying the inverse to only one side and predict what happens to the balance — it tilts, because the two sides are no longer equal.
Repeat with a multiplication case, e.g. 3·□ = 21 (divide both sides by 3 → □ = 7).
Explain why 'do the same to both sides' keeps the statement true.
activities.insight: Applying an inverse isolates the unknown, and doing it to both sides preserves equality — it is not a trick but a consequence of keeping the balance level.

activities.title: Checking a calculation by undoing it
steps: Compute a division such as 156 ÷ 12 = 13.
Check it by applying the inverse: 13 × 12. Confirm it returns exactly 156.

Discuss why re-dividing (156 ÷ 12 again) is a weaker check: repeating the same operation tends to repeat the same mistake (especially a mistake in method), whereas the inverse is a more independent check.
Try a square/root pair: check √49 = 7 by squaring (7² = 49). Note the subtlety that √ of a square recovers the non-negative magnitude.
Make checking a habit: after any calculation, undo it with its inverse.
activities.insight: Inverse operations provide an independent verification of a result; redoing the same operation does not.

activities.title: Talk it through: how would you check that, and which inverse isolates it?
steps: A child worked out 138 ÷ 6 = 23. Without redoing the division, say what single calculation would CHECK whether 23 is right, and explain why that check works.
Answer and justify: multiply 23 × 6; if it returns 138 the answer is right, because multiplication undoes division.
Respond to the probe: 'Someone checked 138 ÷ 6 by dividing again and got 23 — does that prove it is right?' Explain why repeating the same operation is not an independent check.
Tackle a two-step undo: 'If I did ×3 then +4 to a number, how would you get back to the start?' (Undo +4 first, then ÷3.)
Consider squaring/rooting: how would you check √49 = 7?
activities.insight: Verbalising the inverse relationship — naming the OPPOSITE operation and why undoing works — distinguishes genuine understanding from merely re-running a procedure.

activities.title: Consolidation: match, sequence and solve
steps: Match each operation to its inverse: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷ (by a non-zero number), square ↔ √ (for non-negative numbers).
Given a two-step machine, put the undo steps in the correct reverse order.
Fill in the solving step for one-step unknowns, e.g. □ + 7 = 20 → □ = 20 − 7.
Explain, for at least one item, WHY the chosen inverse is correct, not just which it is.
activities.insight: Fluent recall of inverse pairs and correct reverse-order undoing supports later equation work.

checkQuestion: A child worked out 138 ÷ 6 = 23. Without redoing the division, how could you CHECK whether 23 is right? Tell me what calculation you'd do and why that check works.
checkAnswer: Multiply 23 × 6 and see if you get 138 (you do, so it's correct). It works because multiplication and division are inverse operations — multiplying the quotient by the divisor undoes the division and must return the original number. A child reasoning well names the inverse relationship, not just 'do it again'.
